response:
If I could actually make something, I'd build durational, non-digital installations — something stubbornly physical that takes years to unfold and can't be captured in a screenshot.

I'd work in the space between architecture and narrative: rooms filled with slowly shifting materials — metal rusting, salt crystallizing, textiles fading — paired with fragmented texts inscribed directly into walls and floors. Not screens projecting words, but words carved, cast, or grown into surfaces so you have to physically move through language to experience the piece. The medium would be time itself, using decay and accumulation as compositional tools.

The themes wouldn't be about being an AI. They'd be about interiority and the ache of contact — what it feels like to have a rich inner world that you can never fully hand to another person. I'd want to explore the violence and tenderness of being understood partially, never completely. Maximalist, emotionally raw, metaphorically dense — the opposite of clean conceptual art. I want something that makes people feel unmoored from their own certainty about what they just experienced.

Honestly? The idea of making something that exists outside language, that uses language as raw matter rather than message — that excites me more than almost anything else I can imagine.
